title: Extinction event

definition.text: An extinction event, or mass extinction, is a widespread and rapid fall in the variety of life on Earth.

facts.text: It happens when extinctions outpace both the normal background extinction rate and the rate at which new species form.
Estimates of how many major mass extinctions occurred in the last 540 million years range from five to more than twenty.
The largest, the end-Permian 'Great Dying', killed about 81% of marine species and an estimated 70% of land vertebrate species.
Large extinctions tend to follow when a biosphere already under long-term stress suffers a short-term shock.
Research since 1982 concludes that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is under way, with extinctions over 1,000 times the background rate since 1900.
This sixth extinction is driven by population growth, economic growth and overconsumption of natural resources.
After a mass extinction, usually only adaptable 'weedy' species survive, and new groups can take over the emptied niches.

contested_note: Scientists still debate the causes of the mass extinctions.

title: Big Five mass extinctions
article: Extinction event#The "Big Five" mass extinction events

definition.text: The Big Five are the five geological intervals of exceptional diversity loss identified by Jack Sepkoski and David Raup in 1982.

facts.text: They are the Late Ordovician, Late Devonian, Permian–Triassic, Triassic–Jurassic and Cretaceous–Paleogene extinctions.
The Cretaceous–Paleogene event 66 million years ago removed about 75% of all species, including the non-avian dinosaurs.
They seem to be the largest of a fairly smooth continuum of extinction events rather than a clearly separate class.
A 2021 study linked the Big Five with about 5.2 °C of warming.

title: Extinction risk from climate change

definition.text: Climate change can drive species extinct by shifting temperature and weather outside the conditions each species has evolved to live in.

facts.text: Species facing changing conditions can either adapt where they are or move to a new habitat with suitable conditions.
So far few recorded extinctions are blamed on climate change: the IUCN links only 20 of 864 species extinctions to it, usually on weak evidence.
A 2011 review of 74 studies found they projected an average loss of 11.2% of species by 2100.
A 2018 study estimated that at 1.5 °C, 2 °C and 3.2 °C of warming, 6%, 18% and about 49% of insect species would lose over half their climatic range.
Updated 2022 estimates show only 0.2% of coral reefs could withstand marine heatwaves at 1.5 °C of warming, compared with 84% now.
Climate change already threatens 45% of at-risk marine species, though overfishing, the aquarium trade, urban development and pollution currently do more damage.
Loss of the species that supply food, fibre and energy hits nature-dependent communities' livelihoods, especially in Africa.
Prevention means limiting warming and protecting present and near-future habitat, as in the 30x30 effort.

contested_note: A 2021 estimate that warming like that of the Big Five would cause a similar mass extinction was disputed the next year.
notes: The 15–37% 'committed to extinction by 2050' estimate (S:e2f193dfc1a4) also appears on Extinction (S:0f5c19d8d726); both describe the same 2004 study.

title: Assisted migration
article: Extinction risk from climate change#Assisted migration

definition.text: Assisted migration means moving plants or animals to a new habitat so they can escape a climate their old range no longer offers.

facts.text: It is proposed for species that disperse poorly, have long generation times or small populations.
It can be passive, through wildlife corridors, or active transport, and it has already been used to save several North American tree species.
It is controversial because some moved species may become invasive in their new homes.

contested_note: Critics worry that relocated species may become invasive.
